claim: Somatic genetic heterogeneity resulting from post-zygotic DNA mutations is widespread in human tissues and can cause diseases.
source: Somatic genetic heterogeneity resulting from post-zygotic DNA mutations is widespread in human tissues and can cause diseases, however, few studies have investigated its role in neurodegenerative processes such as Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence: This is a general statement about somatic mosaicism supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: Few studies have investigated the role of somatic genetic heterogeneity in neurodegenerative processes such as Alzheimer's disease.
source: Somatic genetic heterogeneity resulting from post-zygotic DNA mutations is widespread in human tissues and can cause diseases, however, few studies have investigated its role in neurodegenerative processes such as Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence: This claim is supported by the literature review in the introduction indicating limited prior research.

claim: Microglia from AD patients are selectively enriched for pathogenic variants that are not present in neuronal, glia/stromal cells, or blood compared to age-matched controls.
source: Here, we report the selective enrichment of microglia clones carrying pathogenic variants, that are not present in neuronal, glia/stromal cells, or blood, from patients with AD in comparison to age-matched controls.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the targeted deep sequencing data presented in the results section.

claim: Microglia-specific AD-associated variants preferentially target the MAPK pathway.
source: Notably, microglia-specific AD-associated variants preferentially target the MAPK pathway, including recurrent CBL ring-domain mutations.
evidence: This finding is supported by pathway enrichment analysis and the identification of specific variants in MAPK pathway genes.

claim: Recurrent CBL ring-domain mutations are found in microglia from AD patients.
source: Notably, microglia-specific AD-associated variants preferentially target the MAPK pathway, including recurrent CBL ring-domain mutations.
evidence: This is supported by the identification of CBL variants in six patients as shown in the results.

claim: AD-associated microglia variants activate ERK.
source: These variants activate ERK and drive a microglia transcriptional program characterized by a strong neuro-inflammatory response, both in vitro and in patients.
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot experiments showing increased ERK phosphorylation in cells expressing the variants.

claim: AD-associated microglia variants drive a microglia transcriptional program characterized by a strong neuro-inflammatory response in vitro and in patients.
source: These variants activate ERK and drive a microglia transcriptional program characterized by a strong neuro-inflammatory response, both in vitro and in patients.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data from cell lines and patient samples showing inflammatory signatures.

claim: Microglial expression of a MAPK pathway activating variant causes neurodegeneration in mice.
source: Although the natural history of AD-associated microglial clones is difficult to establish in humans, microglial expression of a MAPK pathway activating variant was previously shown to cause neurodegeneration in mice, suggesting that AD-associated neuroinflammatory microglial clones may contribute to the neurodegenerative process in patients.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study (Mass et al., 2017).

claim: AD-associated neuroinflammatory microglial clones may contribute to the neurodegenerative process in patients.
source: Although the natural history of AD-associated microglial clones is difficult to establish in humans, microglial expression of a MAPK pathway activating variant was previously shown to cause neurodegeneration in mice, suggesting that AD-associated neuroinflammatory microglial clones may contribute to the neurodegenerative process in patients.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the mouse model data and the findings in human patients.

claim: AD is diagnosed in approximately 90% of progressive dementia cases.
source: AD is diagnosed in ~90% of cases, with an estimated prevalence of ~10% in the population over 65 y of age (Hebert et al., 2013; Alzheimer's Association, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: AD has an estimated prevalence of approximately 10% in the population over 65 years of age.
source: AD is diagnosed in ~90% of cases, with an estimated prevalence of ~10% in the population over 65 y of age (Hebert et al., 2013; Alzheimer's Association, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Autosomal dominant forms of AD due to rare germline variants with high penetrance account for an estimated approximately 1% of cases.
source: Although autosomal dominant forms of AD due to rare germline variants with high penetrance account only for an estimated ~1% of cases (Lanoiselée et al., 2017; Goate et al., 1991; Chartier-Harlin et al., 1991; Levy-Lahad et al., 1995a; Levy-Lahad et al., 1995b; Rogaev et al., 1995), a number of common variants were also shown to contribute to disease risk.
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: Carriers of one germline copy of the APOE4 allele have a threefold higher risk of AD.
source: Carriers of one germline copy of the epsilon4 (E4) allele of the apolipoprotein E gene (APOE4), present in ~15 to 20% of the population, have a threefold higher risk of AD, while two copies (~2 to 3% of the population) increase the risk by ~10 fold (Saunders et al., 1993; Murrell et al., 2006; Sando et al., 2008; Lumsden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic association studies.

claim: Carriers of two copies of the APOE4 allele have approximately a 10-fold increased risk of AD.
source: Carriers of one germline copy of the epsilon4 (E4) allele of the apolipoprotein E gene (APOE4), present in ~15 to 20% of the population, have a threefold higher risk of AD, while two copies (~2 to 3% of the population) increase the risk by ~10 fold (Saunders et al., 1993; Murrell et al., 2006; Sando et al., 2008; Lumsden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic association studies.

claim: The APOE4 allele is present in approximately 15 to 20% of the population.
source: Carriers of one germline copy of the epsilon4 (E4) allele of the apolipoprotein E gene (APOE4), present in ~15 to 20% of the population, have a threefold higher risk of AD, while two copies (~2 to 3% of the population) increase the risk by ~10 fold (Saunders et al., 1993; Murrell et al., 2006; Sando et al., 2008; Lumsden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to population genetics studies.

claim: Genome-wide association studies have identified approximately 50 common germline variants that moderately increase the risk of AD.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified an additional ~50 common germline variants that more moderately increase the risk of AD, including TREM2, CD33, and MS4A6A variants (Jonsson et al., 2013; Guerreiro et al., 2013; McQuade and Blurton-Jones, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to GWAS studies.

claim: The APOE4 allele is responsible for an increased inflammatory and neurotoxic response of microglia and astrocytes in the brain of carriers.
source: Interestingly, the APOE4 allele is responsible for an increased inflammatory and neurotoxic response of microglia and astrocytes in the brain of carriers (Arnaud et al., 2022; Serrano-Pozo et al., 2021; Rodriguez et al., 2014), and it was noted that the majority of the other germline AD-risk variants are located within or near genes expressed in microglia McQuade and Blurton-Jones, 2019 and in particular at microglia-specific enhancers (Nott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The majority of germline AD-risk variants are located within or near genes expressed in microglia.
source: Interestingly, the APOE4 allele is responsible for an increased inflammatory and neurotoxic response of microglia and astrocytes in the brain of carriers (Arnaud et al., 2022; Serrano-Pozo et al., 2021; Rodriguez et al., 2014), and it was noted that the majority of the other germline AD-risk variants are located within or near genes expressed in microglia McQuade and Blurton-Jones, 2019 and in particular at microglia-specific enhancers (Nott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies.

claim: Germline AD-risk variants are located at microglia-specific enhancers.
source: Interestingly, the APOE4 allele is responsible for an increased inflammatory and neurotoxic response of microglia and astrocytes in the brain of carriers (Arnaud et al., 2022; Serrano-Pozo et al., 2021; Rodriguez et al., 2014), and it was noted that the majority of the other germline AD-risk variants are located within or near genes expressed in microglia McQuade and Blurton-Jones, 2019 and in particular at microglia-specific enhancers (Nott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an epigenomic study.

claim: Genetic variation in microglia may contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodegeneration and AD.
source: These data, together with transcriptional studies (Krasemann et al., 2017; Mathys et al., 2019; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017) support the hypothesis that genetic variation in microglia may contribute to the pathogenesis of neurodegeneration and AD.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple lines of evidence from the literature.

claim: Somatic genetic heterogeneity is a cause of tumoral, developmental, and immune diseases.
source: Somatic genetic heterogeneity (mosaicism), resulting from post-zygotic DNA mutations, is widespread in human tissues, and a cause of tumoral, developmental, and immune diseases (Miller et al., 2021; Martincorena et al., 2015; Martincorena and Campbell, 2015; Behjati et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on somatic mosaicism.

claim: The role of somatic variants in neuropsychiatric disorders is suspected.
source: Additionally, the role of somatic variants in neuropsychiatric disorders is also suspected (McConnell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Mosaicism has been documented in the brain tissue of AD patients in several deep-sequencing studies.
source: Mosaicism has been documented in the brain tissue of AD patients in several deep-sequencing studies (Keogh et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019), showing that the enrichment of putative pathogenic somatic mutations in the PI3K-AKT, MAPK, and AMPK pathway do occur in the brain of patients in comparison to controls (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to sequencing studies.

claim: Enrichment of putative pathogenic somatic mutations in the PI3K-AKT, MAPK, and AMPK pathways occurs in the brain of AD patients compared to controls.
source: Mosaicism has been documented in the brain tissue of AD patients in several deep-sequencing studies (Keogh et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2019; Park et al., 2019), showing that the enrichment of putative pathogenic somatic mutations in the PI3K-AKT, MAPK, and AMPK pathway do occur in the brain of patients in comparison to controls (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific sequencing study.

claim: Previous studies on somatic variants in AD brain tissue lacked cellular resolution and mechanistic insights.
source: However, these studies performed in whole brain tissue lacked cellular resolution and mechanistic insights, and the role of somatic mutants in neurodegenerative diseases remains poorly understood (Miller et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior literature supported by citation.

claim: Somatic variants that activate the PI3K-AKT-mTOR or MAPK pathways in neural progenitors are a cause of cortical dysplasia and epilepsy.
source: Somatic variants that activate the PI3K-AKT-mTOR or MAPK pathways in neural progenitors are a cause of cortical dysplasia and epilepsy D'Gama et al., 2017; Khoshkhoo et al., 2023; Koh et al., 2018; Lim et al., 2015 and developmental brain malformations (Poduri et al., 2012), while somatic variants that activate the MAPK pathway in brain endothelial cells are associated with arteriovenous malformations (Nikolaev et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical and genetic studies.

claim: Somatic variants that activate the MAPK pathway in brain endothelial cells are associated with arteriovenous malformations.
source: Somatic variants that activate the PI3K-AKT-mTOR or MAPK pathways in neural progenitors are a cause of cortical dysplasia and epilepsy D'Gama et al., 2017; Khoshkhoo et al., 2023; Koh et al., 2018; Lim et al., 2015 and developmental brain malformations (Poduri et al., 2012), while somatic variants that activate the MAPK pathway in brain endothelial cells are associated with arteriovenous malformations (Nikolaev et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Expression of a somatic variant activating the MAPK pathway in microglia causes neurodegeneration in mice.
source: Interestingly, we reported that expression of a somatic variant activating the MAPK pathway in microglia causes neurodegeneration in mice (Mass et al., 2017), but the presence and contribution of microglial somatic clones in neurodegenerative diseases and AD remains unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The presence and contribution of microglial somatic clones in neurodegenerative diseases and AD remains unknown.
source: Interestingly, we reported that expression of a somatic variant activating the MAPK pathway in microglia causes neurodegeneration in mice (Mass et al., 2017), but the presence and contribution of microglial somatic clones in neurodegenerative diseases and AD remains unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Human microglia develop in embryos and renew by local proliferation within the brain.
source: Human microglia are reported to develop in embryos and renew by local proliferation within the brain (Askew et al., 2017; Réu et al., 2017; Bian et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental biology studies.

claim: Bone marrow-derived myeloid cells can enter the brain during pathological processes.
source: However, bone marrow-derived myeloid cells can enter the brain, in particular during pathological processes, and may not be distinguishable from resident microglia by transcriptomics alone Kim, 2023.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The study examined post-mortem frozen brain samples and matching blood from 45 patients with intermediate-onset sporadic AD and 44 control individuals.
source: We examined post-mortem frozen brain samples and matching blood from 45 patients with intermediate-onset sporadic AD and 44 control individuals who died of other causes, including 27 donors age and sex-matched donors with the AD cohort (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the study cohort and is supported by the data in Figure 1A and supplementary materials.

claim: APOE risk allele frequency for patients and controls was comparable to published series.
source: APOE risk allele frequency for patients and controls was comparable to published series (Murrell et al., 2006; Sando et al., 2008; Lumsden et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and analysis of germline mutations did not identify deleterious variants in the 140 genes associated with neurological diseases.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to published data and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Analysis of germline mutations did not identify deleterious variants in the 140 genes associated with neurological diseases.
source: APOE risk allele frequency for patients and controls was comparable to published series (Murrell et al., 2006; Sando et al., 2008; Lumsden et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and analysis of germline mutations did not identify deleterious variants in the 140 genes associated with neurological diseases.
evidence: This is a finding from the genetic analysis of the cohort.

claim: Approximately 94% of PU.1+ nuclei correspond to microglia.
source: Single nuclei (sn)RNA-seq was performed on PU.1+ nuclei from one control and three AD patients to evaluate microglia enrichment following PU.1+ purification, and a cell-type annotation analysis indicated that ~94% of PU.1+ nuclei correspond to microglia (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–1H).
evidence: This is supported by single-nuclei RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A total of 744 DNA samples from blood, PU.1+ nuclei, NeuN+ nuclei, and Double Negative nuclei from patients and controls were submitted to targeted deep-DNA sequencing.
source: A total of 744 DNA samples from blood, PU.1+ nuclei, NeuN+ nuclei, and Double Negative nuclei (glia/stromal cells) from patients and controls (Figure 1A) were submitted to targeted hybridization/capture and deep-DNA targeted sequencing (TDS, Figure 1D, see Materials and methods), at mean coverage of ~1100 x (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), for a panel of 716 genes (3.43 Mb, referred to below as BRAIN-PACT) which included genes reported to carry somatic variants in clonal proliferative disorders (n=576 genes) Cheng et al., 2015; Durham et al., 2019 or that have been reported to be associated with neurodegenerativediseases (n=140) (Bras et al., 2012; Renton et al., 2014; Karch et al., 2014; Karch and Goate, 2015; Turner et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Kouri et al., 2015; Scholz and Bras, 2015; Nalls et al., 2014; Supplementary file 2, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the sequencing methodology and is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The mean sequencing coverage was approximately 1100x.
source: A total of 744 DNA samples from blood, PU.1+ nuclei, NeuN+ nuclei, and Double Negative nuclei (glia/stromal cells) from patients and controls (Figure 1A) were submitted to targeted hybridization/capture and deep-DNA targeted sequencing (TDS, Figure 1D, see Materials and methods), at mean coverage of ~1100 x (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), for a panel of 716 genes (3.43 Mb, referred to below as BRAIN-PACT) which included genes reported to carry somatic variants in clonal proliferative disorders (n=576 genes) Cheng et al., 2015; Durham et al., 2019 or that have been reported to be associated with neurodegenerativediseases (n=140) (Bras et al., 2012; Renton et al., 2014; Karch et al., 2014; Karch and Goate, 2015; Turner et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Kouri et al., 2015; Scholz and Bras, 2015; Nalls et al., 2014; Supplementary file 2, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a technical detail of the sequencing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The BRAIN-PACT panel included 716 genes covering 3.43 Mb.
source: A total of 744 DNA samples from blood, PU.1+ nuclei, NeuN+ nuclei, and Double Negative nuclei (glia/stromal cells) from patients and controls (Figure 1A) were submitted to targeted hybridization/capture and deep-DNA targeted sequencing (TDS, Figure 1D, see Materials and methods), at mean coverage of ~1100 x (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), for a panel of 716 genes (3.43 Mb, referred to below as BRAIN-PACT) which included genes reported to carry somatic variants in clonal proliferative disorders (n=576 genes) Cheng et al., 2015; Durham et al., 2019 or that have been reported to be associated with neurodegenerativediseases (n=140) (Bras et al., 2012; Renton et al., 2014; Karch et al., 2014; Karch and Goate, 2015; Turner et al., 2013; Ferrari et al., 2015; Kouri et al., 2015; Scholz and Bras, 2015; Nalls et al., 2014; Supplementary file 2, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the gene panel used for sequencing.

claim: Variant calling using ShearwaterML and Mutect1 identified 826 somatic single-nucleotide-variations at an allelic frequency >0.3%.
source: After QC and filtering of germline variants, variant calling using ShearwaterML, and a curated Mutect1 analysis identified 826 somatic synonymous and non-synonymous single-nucleotide-variations (SNVs), at an allelic frequency >0.3% (mean 1.3%) in the 744 samples, corresponding to an overall variant burden of 0.3 mut/Mb (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary result from the sequencing analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The overall variant burden was 0.3 mutations per megabase.
source: After QC and filtering of germline variants, variant calling using ShearwaterML, and a curated Mutect1 analysis identified 826 somatic synonymous and non-synonymous single-nucleotide-variations (SNVs), at an allelic frequency >0.3% (mean 1.3%) in the 744 samples, corresponding to an overall variant burden of 0.3 mut/Mb (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is calculated from the sequencing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Droplet digital-PCR confirmed approximately 90% of tested variants.
source: Droplet digital-PCR performed on pre-amplification DNA for ~10% of the 760 unique SNV was positive in 90% of cases (Figure 1E; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This validation data is shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 3.

claim: 96 unique SNVs were classified as pathogenic.
source: After annotation using the OncoKB Chakravarty et al., 2017 and ClinVar (Landrum et al., 2014) databases for disease-associated or causative variants (Figure 2D and F; Supplementary file 3), 96 unique SNV were classified as Pathogenic (P)-SNV.
evidence: This is based on annotation using established databases as shown in Figure 2D and F.

claim: 95% of tested pathogenic SNVs were confirmed by droplet digital-PCR.
source: 40% of these P-SNV were tested by droplet digital-PCR and confirmed in 95% of cases (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This validation data is shown in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Most SNVs and pathogenic SNVs were cell-type or tissue-specific.
source: A venn-diagram analysis of SNVs detected in PU.1+, NeuN+, DN, and blood samples indicated that most (>90%) SNV and P-SNV were cell-type or tissue-specific, with ~5% of SNV and ~8% of P-SNV shared between the blood and brain of individual donors (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This analysis is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Approximately 5% of SNVs and 8% of pathogenic SNVs were shared between blood and brain.
source: A venn-diagram analysis of SNVs detected in PU.1+, NeuN+, DN, and blood samples indicated that most (>90%) SNV and P-SNV were cell-type or tissue-specific, with ~5% of SNV and ~8% of P-SNV shared between the blood and brain of individual donors (Figure 1F; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This analysis is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Infiltrating myeloid cells of peripheral origin account for approximately 5% of microglia somatic diversity.
source: These data indicate that targeted deep-sequencing of purified nuclei allows to detect of clonal mosaic variants with high sensitivity and specificity. In addition, 'bar-coding' of clonal variants across tissues suggests that infiltrating myeloid cells of peripheral origin account for ~5% of microglia somatic diversity, and therefore that blood clones have a detectable but minor contribution to microglia, consistent with its local maintenance and proliferation (Askew et al., 2017; Réu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the data on shared variants between blood and brain.

claim: Clonal diversity of blood and PU.1+ nuclei was higher than for DN and neurons.
source: Somatic clonal diversity of the different cell types, as evaluated by the SNV/megabase burden was higher in blood (1 mut/Mb) and PU.1+ nuclei (0.5 mut/Mb) than for DN and neurons (0.18 mut/Mb) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The SNV/mb burden of blood and PU.1+ nuclei increased as a function of age.
source: The SNV/mb burden of blood and PU.1+ nuclei increased as a function of age (Figure 2A and Supplementary file 3) as previously reported for proliferating cells (Martincorena et al., 2015; Martincorena et al., 2018; Jaiswal et al., 2014; Genovese et al., 2014).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 2A and is consistent with published literature.

claim: The SNV/mb burden of blood cells from age-matched controls was higher than for AD patients.
source: Interestingly, the SNV/mb burden of blood cells from age-matched controls was higher than for AD patients (Figure 2B).
evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no difference in SNV/mb burden between PU.1+, NEUN+, and DN samples from AD patients and age-matched controls.
source: In contrast, there was no difference in SNV/mb burden between PU.1+, NEUN+, and DN samples from AD patients and age-matched controls (Figure 2B), and between PU.1+ nuclei from the cortex, hippocampus, and brainstem/cerebellum samples (Figure 2C).
evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no difference in SNV/mb burden between PU.1+ nuclei from different brain regions.
source: In contrast, there was no difference in SNV/mb burden between PU.1+, NEUN+, and DN samples from AD patients and age-matched controls (Figure 2B), and between PU.1+ nuclei from the cortex, hippocampus, and brainstem/cerebellum samples (Figure 2C).
evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Clonal hematopoiesis is inversely associated with the risk of AD.
source: This is consistent with recent studies showing that clonal hematopoiesis is associated with a higher risk of several diseases related to ageing such as cardiovascular diseases, but is inversely associated with the risk of AD (Jaiswal and Ebert, 2019; Bouzid et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Increased pathogenic SNV burden was correlated with age.
source: In contrast to the global SNV burden, increased P-SNV burden was correlated not only with age (Figure 2D), but also with the disease status (AD) (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Increased pathogenic SNV burden was correlated with AD disease status.
source: In contrast to the global SNV burden, increased P-SNV burden was correlated not only with age (Figure 2D), but also with the disease status (AD) (Figure 2E–H).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figures 2E-H.

claim: The pathogenic SNV burden per Mb was selectively and highly enriched in PU.1+ samples from AD patients compared to age-matched controls (p=0.0003).
source: The P-SNV burden per Mb was selectively and highly enriched in PU.1+ samples from AD patients in comparison to age-matched controls (p=0.0003, Figure 2E).
evidence: This statistical comparison is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The pathogenic SNV/Mb burden was similar between brain regions within each group.
source: Analysis of PU1+ P-SNV/Mb burden per brains region indicated that the P-SNV/Mb burden was similar between brain regions within each group (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), and therefore attributable to AD status rather than sampling bias.
evidence: This analysis is shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Microglial clones carrying pathogenic SNVs were enriched in the brain of AD patients compared to age-matched controls.
source: Analysis of mutational load per donor confirmed that microglial clones carrying P-SNV were enriched in the brain of AD patients in comparison to age-matched controls (Figure 2G).
evidence: This analysis is shown in Figure 2G.

claim: A logistic regression analysis confirmed the association between the presence of pathogenic SNVs in PU.1+ nuclei and AD after adjusting for sex and age (OR = 7; p=0.0035).
source: Despite the relatively modest cohort size, a logistic regression analysis confirmed the association between the presence of P-SNVs in PU.1+ nuclei and AD after adjusting for sex and age (OR = 7; p=0.0035, Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This statistical analysis is shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A mixed-effects linear regression model showed an excess of pathogenic SNVs in AD independently of the effect of age (p=0.0215).
source: A mixed-effects linear regression model analysis also showed an excess of P-SNVs in AD independently of the effect of age (p=0.0215) (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This statistical analysis is shown in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Genes targeted by pathogenic SNVs were all expressed in microglia.
source: In addition, genes targeted by P-SNV were all expressed in microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 3) and the analysis of P-SNV/Mb mutational load restricted to genes that are not expressed in microglia did not show an enrichment of candidate pathogenic variants in AD patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 3.

claim: Analysis of pathogenic SNV/Mb mutational load restricted to genes not expressed in microglia did not show enrichment in AD patients.
source: In addition, genes targeted by P-SNV were all expressed in microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F and Supplementary file 3) and the analysis of P-SNV/Mb mutational load restricted to genes that are not expressed in microglia did not show an enrichment of candidate pathogenic variants in AD patients (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This control analysis is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The most significant pathways enriched for genes carrying pathogenic SNVs in microglia from AD patients were the receptor tyrosine kinase/MAP-Kinase pathways.
source: Pathways analysis of genes carrying P-SNV in microglia from AD patients, against the background of the 716 genes sequenced, showed that the most significant pathways enriched were the receptor tyrosine kinase/MAP-Kinase pathways (Reactome, GO, and canonical pathways, Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4), corresponding to pathogenic/oncogenic variants in 6 of the 15 genes of the classical MAPK pathway (Rauen, 2013) (CBL, BRAF, RIT1, NF1, PTPN11, KRAS), TEK, and the KEGG Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) pathway, which includes the former plus SMAD5 and TP53 (Figure 3B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This pathway analysis is shown in Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4.

claim: Pathogenic/oncogenic variants were found in 6 of the 15 genes of the classical MAPK pathway in AD patients.
source: Pathways analysis of genes carrying P-SNV in microglia from AD patients, against the background of the 716 genes sequenced, showed that the most significant pathways enriched were the receptor tyrosine kinase/MAP-Kinase pathways (Reactome, GO, and canonical pathways, Figure 3A and Supplementary file 4), corresponding to pathogenic/oncogenic variants in 6 of the 15 genes of the classical MAPK pathway (Rauen, 2013) (CBL, BRAF, RIT1, NF1, PTPN11, KRAS), TEK, and the KEGG Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) pathway, which includes the former plus SMAD5 and TP53 (Figure 3B, C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Mutational load for MAPK genes was significantly higher in AD patients compared to age-matched controls.
source: Mutational load for MAPK genes was significantly higher in AD patients in comparison to age-matched control (Figure 3C).
evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Pathogenic SNVs targeting genes of the classical RTK/MAPK pathway were detected in PU.1+ samples from approximately 25% of AD patients tested (p=0.0145 vs age-matched controls).
source: P-SNV targeting genes of the classical RTK/MAPK pathway (Figure 3C) were detected in the PU.1+ samples from ~25% of the AD patients tested (p=0.0145 vs age-matched controls, Figure 3D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Six patients (13% of AD patients) carried recurrent pathogenic SNVs in the RING domain of CBL.
source: Strikingly, half of these patients (six patients, 13% of AD patients in this series) carried recurrent P-SNV in the RING domain of CBL (Schnittger et al., 2012; Fernandes et al., 2010; Sargin et al., 2007; Dunbar et al., 2008; Bernard et al., 2014; Loh et al., 2009; Grand et al., 2009; Klampfl et al., 2013; Niemeyer et al., 2010; Javadi et al., 2013; Ogawa, 2019; Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3B-E.

claim: Two patients presented with pathogenic SNVs in the Switch II domain of RIT1.
source: Two additional patients presented with P-SNV in the Switch II domain of RIT1 (Gómez-Seguí et al., 2013; Figure 3B–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3B-F.

claim: CBL RING-domain variants found in AD patients increased MAPK phosphorylation in response to EGF.
source: We confirmed that CBL RING-domain variants found in AD patients increased MAPK phosphorylation in response to EGF upon expression of HA-tagged WT or mutant alleles in HEK293T cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This functional validation is shown in Figure 3E.

claim: RIT1 variants found in AD patients increased MAPK phosphorylation in response to FBS in HEK293T cells.
source: As in the case of CBL variants, the 2 RIT1 variants found in AD patients increased MAPK phosphorylation in response to FBS in HEK293T cells expressing these mutant alleles (Figure 3F).
evidence: This functional validation is shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Approximately 27% of AD patients in this series present with microglial clones carrying one or several oncogenic variants that activate the RTK/MAPK pathway.
source: These data altogether indicate that a subset of AD patients (12/45, ~27% of this series) present with microglial clones carrying one or several oncogenic variants that activate the RTK/MAPK pathway, and are characterized by recurrent oncogenic variants in CBL and RIT1.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings on MAPK pathway variants.

claim: The allelic frequencies of MAPK activating variants in brain samples from AD patients range from approximately 1-6% in microglia.
source: The allelic frequencies at which MAPK activating variants are detected in brain samples from AD patients range from ~1–6% in microglia (Figure 3G), which correspond to mutant clones representing 2 to 12% of all microglia in these samples, assuming heterozygosity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The allelic frequency range of MAPK activating variants in AD patients is comparable to that observed for BRAFV600E in microglia from histiocytosis patients.
source: This range of allelic frequency is frequently observed for the MAPK-activating BRAFV600E variant in microglia isolated from brain samples of six patients diagnosed with BRAFV600E+ histiocytosis, a rare clonal myeloid disorder associated with neurodegeneration (Mass et al., 2017; Boyd et al., 2020; Bhatia et al., 2020; Diamond et al., 2016; Héritier et al., 2018; Figure 3G and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This comparison is shown in Figure 3G.

claim: CBL variants increased ERK phosphorylation upon lentiviral transduction in BV2 murine microglial cells.
source: CBL variants increased ERK phosphorylation upon lentiviral transduction in BV2 murine microglial cells (Blasi et al., 1990; Henn et al., 2009; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MAC lines expressing CBL, RIT1, KRAS, and PTPN11 variants presented with increased ERK phosphorylation and/or increased proliferation.
source: MAC lines expressing CBL, RIT1, KRAS, and PTPN11 variants presented with increased ERK phosphorylation and/or increontrols, as measured by Western immunoblotting and EdU incorporation (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Hallmark and KEGG pathway analysis of RNAseq data from mutant MAC lines showed increased RAS, TNF, IL6, JAK STAT signaling, complement, inflammatory responses, and mTOR pathway activation signatures.
source: In addition, Hallmark and KEGG pathway analysis of RNAseq data from control and mutant lines showed increased RAS, TNF, IL6, and JAK STAT signaling, complement, inflammatory responses, and mTOR pathway activation signatures in mutants (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and Supplementary file 7.

claim: CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells were larger and presented with more lamellipodia than isogenic controls.
source: However, CBL404C/Y cells were larger and presented with more lamellipodia, resulting in an amoeboid morphology less frequently observed in isogenic controls (Figure 4D and E), and their proliferation rate was slightly increased, as measured by EdU incorporation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4D and E.

claim: The proliferation rate of CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells was slightly increased compared to isogenic controls.
source: However, CBL404C/Y cells were larger and presented with more lamellipodia, resulting in an amoeboid morphology less frequently observed in isogenic controls (Figure 4D and E), and their proliferation rate was slightly increased, as measured by EdU incorporation (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ERK phosphorylation after stimulation with CSF-1 was increased by approximately twofold in CBL404C/Y cells compared to isogenic WT.
source: Moreover CBL404C/Y cells cultured in CSF1-supplemented medium also presented with a higher basal pERK level than control when restimulated with CSF1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I), and ERK phosphorylation after stimulation of starved microglia-like cells with CSF-1 was increased by ~ twofold in comparison to isogenic WT (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Heterozygosity for a CBLC404Y allele is sufficient to activate human microglia-like cells increasing their proliferation and ERK activation.
source: Altogether, these results showed that heterozygosity for a CBLC404Y allele is sufficient to activate human microglia-like cells increasing their proliferation and ERK activation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experiments on CBL404C/Y cells.

claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analyses of RNAseq comparing CBL404C/Y and isogenic CBL404C/C microglia-like cells showed upregulation of Glycolysis, Oxidative Phosphorylation, and mTORC1 signatures.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analyses (GSEA) of RNAseq comparing CBL404C/Y and isogenic CBL404C/C microglia-like cells showed upregulation of Glycolysis, Oxidative Phosphorylation, and mTORC1 signatures, indicating increased metabolism and energy consumption by the mutant cells (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 8.

claim: CBL404C/Y cells upregulated complement, TNF, and JAK STAT signaling and inflammatory signatures.
source: In addition, as observed in MAC lines, CBL404C/Y cells upregulated complement, TNF, and JAK STAT signaling and inflammatory signatures (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 8; Ghosh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 8.

claim: Increased production of TNF, IL-6, IFN-γ, IL-1β, C3, and complement Factor H by CBL404C/Y cells was confirmed by ELISA.
source: Increased production of TNF, IL-6, IFN-γ, IL-1β, C3, and complement Factor H (CFH) by CBL404C/Y cells was confirmed by ELISA (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells presented with signatures associated with neurodegenerative disorders from the KEGG database.
source: In addition, CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells also presented with signatures from the KEGG database associated with neurodegenerative disorders (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 8), and for the recently published human microglia AD scRNA-seq signature, obtained by analysis of 24 sporadic AD patients and 24 controls (Mathys et al., 2019; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 8.

claim: CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells showed enrichment for the human AD-microglia snRNA-seq signature.
source: In addition, CBL404C/Y microglia-like cells also presented with signatures from the KEGG database associated with neurodegenerative disorders (Figure 5A; Supplementary file 8), and for the recently published human microglia AD scRNA-seq signature, obtained by analysis of 24 sporadic AD patients and 24 controls (Mathys et al., 2019; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Heterozygosity for the CBLC404Y allele is sufficient to drive expression of a neuroinflammatory/AD signature in human microglia-like cells.
source: These data indicated that heterozygosity for the CBLC404Y allele is sufficient to drive expression of a neuroinflammatory/AD signature in a human microglia-like cell type, characterized by increased metabolism and the production of neurotoxic cytokines known to interfere with normal brain homeostasis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the RNA-seq and ELISA experiments.

claim: Analysis of snRNA-seq data from microglia showed that samples from patients carrying variants were enriched for inflammatory, TNF, mTOR, oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis signatures.
source: Analysis of the snRNA-seq data from five samples of purified microglia nuclei from four donors control, AD without and with pathogenic variants (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–H and Supplementary file 9) using unsupervised Louvain clustering and GSEA showed that microglia samples from patients carrying variants were enriched for the signatures observed in the MAC lines and CBL404C/Y cells (Figure 5D and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5D and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microglia cluster 2 and 2B were most enriched for inflammatory, TNF, mTOR, oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis signatures in patients carrying variants.
source: In particular, microglia cluster 2 and 2B, were most enriched for the inflammatory, TNF, mTOR, and oxidative phosphorylation and glycolysis signatures in patients carrying variants (AD52, AD53) but not the controls (C11, AD34) (Figure 5D and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5D and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: KRAS A59G variant reads were detected in cluster 2/2B from patient AD52.
source: Despite the small size of the mutant clones and the low sensitivity of scRNA-seq to detect rare allelic variants, KRAS A59G variant reads were detected in cluster 2/2B from patient AD52.
evidence: This demonstrates detection of the variant at single-cell resolution.

claim: Patients' microglial clones carrying pathogenic mutations are associated with a metabolic and neuroinflammatory signature that includes the production of neurotoxic cytokines in vitro and in vivo.
source: Altogether, the above results support the hypothesis that patients' microglial clones carrying pathogenic mutations are associated with a metabolic and neuroinflammatory signature that includes the production of neurotoxic cytokines in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating multiple lines of evidence.

claim: Microglia from a cohort of 45 AD patients with intermediate-onset sporadic AD is enriched for clones carrying pathogenic/oncogenic variants in genes associated with clonal proliferative disorders compared to 44 controls.
source: We report here that microglia from a cohort of 45 AD patients with intermediate-onset sporadic AD (mean age 65 y.o) is enriched for clones carrying pathogenic/oncogenic variants in genes associated with clonal proliferative disorders (Supplementary file 2) in comparison to 44 controls.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Pathogenic variants in AD patients are absent from blood, glia, or neurons in most cases.
source: These pathogenic variants are absent from blood, glia, or neurons in most cases.
evidence: This is based on the cell-type specific analysis of variants.

claim: Pathogenic variants in AD patients are found predominantly in the MAPK pathway and include recurrent variants.
source: They are found predominantly in the MAPK pathway and include reccurrent variants (CBL RING domain variants in six patients), which promote microglial proliferation, activation, and expression of a neuroinflammatory/neurodegereration-associated transcriptional program in vitro and in vivo, and the production of neurotoxic cytokines IL1b, TNF, and IFNg (Liu and Quan, 2018; Roy et al., 2020; Jayaraman et al., 2021; Ou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings on MAPK pathway variants and their effects.

claim: Heterozygous expression of pathogenic CBL variant in human microglia-like cells was sufficient to drive a transcriptional program that associates with increased metabolic activity and a neurotoxic inflammatory response.
source: Heterozygous expression of pathogenic CBL variant in human microglia-like cells was sufficient to drive a transcriptional program that associates with increased metabolic activity and a neurotoxic inflammatory response, also observed in microglia from patients with MAPK-activating variants.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the iPSC-derived microglia experiments.

claim: The association between AD and MAPK pathway variants is consistent with a previous study where WES performed on unseparated brain tissue from AD patients showed enrichment for the MAPK pathway.
source: The association between AD and MAPK pathway variants is consistent with a previous study where WES performed on unseparated brain tissue from AD patients showed that putative pathogenic somatic variants were enriched for the MAPK pathway, despite the lower sensitivity of the approach and the lack of cellular specificity (Park et al., 2019).
evidence: This comparison to prior literature supports the findings.

claim: Somatic variants that activate the MAPK pathway in tissue macrophages cause histiocytosis, which is strongly associated with neurodegeneration.
source: In addition, somatic variants that activate the MAPK pathway in tissue macrophages cause a clonal proliferative and inflammatory disease called Histiocytosis, strongly associated with neurodegeneration (Mass et al., 2017; Boyd et al., 2020; Bhatia et al., 2020; Diamond et al., 2016), and introduction in mouse microglia of the variant allele most frequently associated with histiocytosis (BRAFV600E) causes neurodegeneration in mice (Mass et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on histiocytosis.

claim: Introduction of BRAFV600E in mouse microglia causes neurodegeneration in mice.
source: In addition, somatic variants that activate the MAPK pathway in tissue macrophages cause a clonal proliferative and inflammatory disease called Histiocytosis, strongly associated with neurodegeneration (Mass et al., 2017; Boyd et al., 2020; Bhatia et al., 2020; Diamond et al., 2016), and introduction in mouse microglia of the variant allele most frequently associated with histiocytosis (BRAFV600E) causes neurodegeneration in mice (Mass et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a mouse model study.

claim: The allelic frequencies of pathogenic variants found in AD patients are within the range of clonal frequencies observed in histiocytosis patients.
source: The allelic frequencies of pathogenic variants found in AD patients are lower than values classically observed in solid tumors or leukemia, but within the range of the clonal frequency of pathogenic T cells observed in auto-immune diseases (Thapa et al., 2015), and we found that they were in the range of the allelic frequencies observed for the BRAFV600E variant in microglia in the brain of Histiocytosis patients.
evidence: This comparison provides context for the observed allelic frequencies.

claim: The RAS/MAPK signaling pathway is involved in microglia proliferation, activation, and inflammatory response.
source: Moreover, the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway is involved in microglia proliferation, activation, and inflammatory response (Lindberg et al., 2014; Qu et al., 2012; Coniglio et al., 2012), neuronal death, neurodegeneration, and AD pathogenesis (McQuade and Blurton-Jones, 2019; Nott et al., 2019; Mass et al., 2017; Scheltens et al., 2018), and its activation has been proposed to be an early event in the pathophysiology of AD in human (Lachén-Montes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Activation of the RAS/MAPK pathway has been proposed to be an early event in the pathophysiology of AD in humans.
source: Moreover, the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway is involved in microglia proliferation, activation, and inflammatory response (Lindberg et al., 2014; Qu et al., 2012; Coniglio et al., 2012), neuronal death, neurodegeneration, and AD pathogenesis (McQuade and Blurton-Jones, 2019; Nott et al., 2019; Mass et al., 2017; Scheltens et al., 2018), and its activation has been proposed to be an early event in the pathophysiology of AD in human (Lachén-Montes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on AD pathophysiology.

claim: Neuroinflammation is an early event in AD pathogenesis and is increasingly considered critical in pathogenesis initiation and progression.
source: Neuroinflammation is an early event in AD pathogenesis, increasingly considered as critical in pathogenesis initiation and progression (Arnaud et al., 2022; Schöll et al., 2015; Kinney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on neuroinflammation in AD.

claim: The main known genetic risk factor for sporadic AD is the APOE4 allele, which is responsible for an increased inflammatory response in the brain of carriers.
source: This is underscored by the observation that the main known genetic risk factor for sporadic AD is the APOE4 allele, responsible for an increased inflammatory response in the brain of APOE4 carriers (Arnaud et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on APOE4.

claim: The contributing role of MAPK activating variants could be comparable to that of the APOE4 allele.
source: In this regard, the contributing role of MAPK activating variants could be comparable to that of the APOE4 allele, and we noted that the allelic frequency of APOE4 allele is lower in patients with pathogenic variants (16/46 alleles, 34%) than in patients without detected variant (23/44 alleles, 53%) although the difference did not reach significance in this series.
evidence: This is a speculative comparison based on the observed data.

claim: The allelic frequency of APOE4 allele is lower in patients with pathogenic variants (34%) than in patients without detected variant (53%).
source: In this regard, the contributing role of MAPK activating variants could be comparable to that of the APOE4 allele, and we noted that the allelic frequency of APOE4 allele is lower in patients with pathogenic variants (16/46 alleles, 34%) than in patients without detected variant (23/44 alleles, 53%) although the difference did not reach significance in this series.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Microglia variants are frequently absent from blood, which does not support a model where blood cells massively infiltrate the brain or replace the microglia pool in patients.
source: Microglia variants are frequently absent from blood, and our DNA sequencing barcoding approach does not support a model where blood cells massively infiltrate the brain or replace the microglia pool in patients from our series, but instead consistent with the local maintenance and proliferation of microglia (Askew et al., 2017; Réu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the analysis of shared variants between blood and brain.

claim: The results are consistent with local maintenance and proliferation of microglia.
source: Microglia variants are frequently absent from blood, and our DNA sequencing barcoding approach does not support a model where blood cells massively infiltrate the brain or replace the microglia pool in patients from our series, but instead consistent with the local maintenance and proliferation of microglia (Askew et al., 2017; Réu et al., 2017).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by the data and citations to studies on microglia biology.

claim: The results are consistent with a recent study showing that clonal hematopoiesis was inversely associated with the risk of AD.
source: In addition, our results are consistent with a recent study showing that clonal hematopoiesis was inversely associated with the risk of AD (Bouzid et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The association of microglia clones carrying pathogenic variants with AD is not a consequence of an overall increase in microglia mutational load in AD.
source: The association of microglia clones carrying pathogenic variants with AD in a subset of patients is not a consequence of an overall increase in microglia mutational load (SNV) in AD.
evidence: This is based on the analysis showing no difference in overall SNV burden but enrichment of pathogenic variants.

claim: Pathogenic microglia clones could contribute to AD pathogenesis together with other genetic and environmental factors.
source: Together with evidence that pathogenic variants drive neuroinflammation, these data suggest that these clones could contribute to AD pathogenesis, together with other genetic and environmental factors.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Lewy bodies, amyloid angiopathy, tauopathy, or alpha synucleinopathy were equally distributed among AD patients with or without microglia clones carrying MAPK activating variants.
source: Lewy bodies, amyloid angiopathy, tauopathy, or alpha synucleinopathy, were equally distributed among AD patients with or without microglia clones carrying MAPK activating variants.
evidence: This is an observation from the clinical data analysis.

claim: The natural history of microglial clones is difficult to study in humans.
source: The natural history of the microglial clones is difficult to study in human.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of studying disease progression in humans.

claim: Microglial clones with proliferative and activation advantages may be present at the onset and contribute to the early stages of AD.
source: It is possible that microglial clones with proliferative and activation advantages and a neuroinflammatory and neurotoxic profile may be present at the onset and contribute to the early stages of the disease.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about disease mechanism.

claim: Microglial clones carrying pathogenic mutations may appear or be selected later during the course of AD in the inflammatory milieu.
source: Alternatively, it is also possible that the microglial clones carrying the pathogenic mutations appear or are selected later during the course of the disease in the inflammatory milieu of the AD brain.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative hypothesis about disease mechanism.

claim: Pathogenic microglial clones may contribute to disease progression, including neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.
source: In the latter case, pathogenic microglial clones may contribute to disease progression, i.e., neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the potential role of the clones.
